author: haiku
reason: A explains the stack and protocol terms someone new would need (Redis, PKCE, nonce, GETDEL, login CSRF, start_session), and its numbered steps follow the diagram in order and say why each check exists, so it reads on its own; B is tighter but assumes more background and contradicts itself (it says a bad state is "the only case that gets an error page" while also sending code-exchange failures to an error page).

author: haiku
reason: B is better for a newcomer because it explains the stack and the protocol: it defines Redis, Postgres, OIDC, PKCE, nonce, GETDEL, bcrypt and sid, and its steps give the reasons for each check, while A assumes the reader already knows these terms, even though A's failure table is somewhat tighter.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines every mechanism a newcomer meets (the bind cookie, the confirm token, start_session, lockout) and explains why each exists, and it walks through the flow in prose so you don't have to decode the mermaid chart. B is tighter but leaves gaps: its confirm step asks for a CSRF token from a user who has no session yet, and it never explains how that works.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer and repeats itself, but it explains things an outsider would not know: what state, nonce, PKCE, the bind cookie and the confirm token are for. It also lists every endpoint in one table and walks through the flow step by step. It covers gaps that A leaves open, such as how the confirm step blocks cross-site requests when the user has no session yet, and what happens when Redis fails.

author: haiku
reason: Document B is quicker to take in for someone new to the project: it opens with a one-paragraph overview, uses a simple diagram, includes a "where the state lives" table and the actual MERGE SQL, and its failure table is short, whereas Document A, though more rigorous about locks and timeout races, buries the main flow under a 30-term glossary and a very busy diagram.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the same pipeline in a tighter, easier-to-follow shape (short glossary, readable diagram, a state-ownership table, clear step-by-step failure handling), so a newcomer gets an accurate mental model quickly, while B's extra rigour (lock, replay-timestamp cutoff, timeout race) is buried in a long glossary, a dense diagram and confusing step ordering such as step 7 starting when step 8 opens.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for an outsider to follow: it walks through the load in numbered steps, each saying what starts it, what it does, what data it touches and what happens if it fails; it shows the merge as concrete SQL; and it names the exact mechanisms (the lock index, the check that the attempt's own row is still running, the REPEATABLE READ snapshot, the checksum formula), where A states the same guarantees in a looser flowchart and prose.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a short summary of the whole system, then walks through each step with what starts it, what it does, what data it touches and what happens when it fails, and it includes the actual merge SQL and the lock mechanism, so a newcomer can understand both the flow and why it is safe more quickly than with B's looser prose.

author: haiku
reason: A opens with a summary that walks through the whole flow and says why the archive, not the log, is the replay source; it then defines every term, numbers each step, and adds a failure table and a verification list, so an outsider can follow and check it more easily than B's harder-to-follow automatic seal and per-collector cutoff.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer the clearer way in: it opens with the existing infrastructure, the whole flow and why the archive is the replay source, and it collects failures in a table plus a verification list, while A's cutoff-and-seal mechanism is rigorous but dense and harder to absorb on a first read.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines the stack concepts an outsider lacks (partitions, offsets, in-sync replicas, the winner rule) and gives the reason behind each fixed rule, such as the 60 s append bound that makes day closing safe and why the lookback is 8 days; B is tighter and has a diagram, but it leaves terms like consumer-group fencing undefined and splits one idea across closed days, seals and stale markers.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives an outsider more to work with: it defines the log terms (partition, offset, in-sync replicas), groups the invariants the design depends on in its own section, and explains why each mechanism exists (the load ledger, keeping IP and User-Agent, the 60-second bound), so I could reason about the system rather than just follow A's tighter but terser steps.

author: haiku
reason: A explains up front why the design has its shape (the 60-second request limit, how the queue retries and redelivers, the multipart part limits) and lays out the data model before the steps, so an outsider can follow the mechanism. B defers its table schema to the build steps, assumes more of the stack, and leaves open whether a large export can finish within three attempts, where A answers it with the job handover.

author: haiku
reason: I'd rather be handed B. It starts with how the page works today, the limits that shape the design (the 60-second API limit, the 30-minute job timeout, 512 MB workers, the 5 MB part minimum) and why the export splits into two paths, and it defines its terms and lays out the data table before the steps. A is tighter and handles some failures more neatly, but it assumes context I don't have ("the brief") and leaves the schema until the end.
